question: 4. Let $k$ be a positive integer, find all polynomials $P(x)=a_{n}+a_{n-1} x+\cdots+a_{0} x^{n}$, where $a_{i}$ are real numbers, that satisfy the equation $P(P(x))=(P(x))^{k}$.

meta.gold_solution:
4. If $P(x)$ is the zero polynomial, then it satisfies the condition. Hereafter, assume $P(x)$ is not the zero polynomial, and let $n$ be the degree of $P(x)$. By comparing the degrees of the polynomials on both sides of the given identity, we get $n^{2}=k n$.
(1) If $n=0$, then $P(x)=C$ (a constant). When $k=1$, $C$ can be any non-zero real number; when $k$ is a positive even number, $C=1$; when $k$ is an odd number greater than 1, $C= \pm 1$.
(2) If $n>0$, then $n=k$. Let $\quad P(x)=a_{0} x^{k}+a_{1} x^{k-1}+\cdots+a_{k} \quad\left(a_{0} \neq 0\right)$,
then we have $a_{0}\left(a_{0} x^{k}+\cdots+a_{k}\right)^{k}+a_{1}\left(a_{0} x^{k}+\cdots+a_{k}\right)^{k-1}+\cdots+a_{k} \equiv\left(a_{0} x^{k}+\cdots+a_{k}\right)^{k}$,
by comparing the coefficients of the highest terms on both sides, we get $a_{0}^{f+1}=a_{\delta}^{\delta}$, so $a_{0}=1$, then the above equation becomes
$$
a_{1}\left(x^{k}+\cdots+a_{k}\right)^{k-1}+\cdots+a_{k} \equiv 0 .
$$

Thus, $a_{1}=a_{2}=\cdots=a_{k} \equiv 0$, hence $P(x)=x^{k}$.

question:
I have 10 balls that look identical on the outside, but one of them is radioactive, and I don't know which one. One of my acquaintances would only buy non-radioactive balls from me, at 1 forint each. Another acquaintance of mine has a device that can determine if there are any radioactive balls among any number of balls. He charges 1 forint per measurement, but his device has the property that if there is a radioactive ball among the measured balls, all of them become radioactive during the measurement.

What is the maximum profit I can definitely achieve?

meta.gold_solution:
(Solution for Az F. 2494.) Generally, for $n \geq 2$ balls, we answer the problem's question. Instead of profit, we examine the loss! This is the sum of the number of measurements and the number of balls that have become radioactive. Our task is to find: what is the smallest possible loss?

Let $H_{k}$ denote the sum of the first $k$ positive integers, i.e., let $H_{k}=\frac{k(k+1)}{2}$, the so-called $k$-th "triangular number". We claim that if $n \leq H_{k}+1$, then there is a measurement procedure in which we lose at most $k+1$ forints, while if $n>H_{k}+1$, then no matter what method we try, it is possible that our loss is at least $k+2$ forints.

Let $n \leq H_{k}+1=k+(k-1)+(k-2)+\ldots+2+2$. Then there exist non-negative integers $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{k-1}$ such that

$$
n=a_{1}+a_{2}+\ldots+a_{k-1}+2
$$

and

$$
a_{1} \leq k, \quad a_{2} \leq k-1, \ldots, a_{k-1} \leq 2
$$

Indeed, if $n=H_{k}+1$, then the choice

$$
n=k+(k-1)+\ldots+2+2
$$

is appropriate, and if $n < H_{k}+1$, we can choose the $a_{i}$ values appropriately to satisfy the conditions.

Now, let $n > H_{k}+1$ and assume there exists a measurement procedure in which the loss is at most $k+1$ forints, regardless of the order of the balls during measurement.

If in the $i$-th measurement we measure $a_{i}$ balls at once, then clearly $a_{i}+2 \leq (k+1)$ must hold, because if the radioactive ball happens to be among these, then with this measurement, our loss is $a_{i}+i$ forints. (We can obviously rule out the possibility that all measured balls are healthy, as we would not perform such a measurement.)

This means that with $l \leq k$ measurements, we can examine at most $k+(k-1)+\ldots+(k-l+1)$ balls. Thus, the number of balls not yet measured is at least

$$
\begin{gathered}
n-(k+(k-1)+\ldots+(k-l+1)) \geq H_{k}+2-(k+(k-1)+\ldots+(k-l+1))= \\
=2+(k-l)+(k-l-1)+\ldots+1 \geq 2+(k-1)
\end{gathered}
$$

After the $i$-th measurement, at least $(k-l)+2$ balls have not been examined. If all balls have been healthy so far and we stop the measurement, our loss is at least $l+(k-l)+2=k+2$ forints. If we measure $(k+1)$-th time and find the radioactive ball(s) only then, the loss is again at least $k+2$ forints.

Thus, we have shown that if $n>H_{k}+1$, then no matter how we try, it is possible that our loss (in the worst case) is at least $(k+2)$ forints.

If $H_{k}$ denotes the smallest triangular number not greater than $(n-1)$, then we can ensure that our loss is $k+1$ forints, but not less. Thus, we can safely count on a profit of at most $n-k-1$ forints. Since $H_{3}=6, H_{4}=10$, for $n=10$, $k=4$, and thus we can count on a profit of at most $10-(4+1)=5$ forints, for example, with the following grouping: $a_{1}=3, a_{2}=3, a_{3}=2, a_{4}=2$.

If $n=100$, then $H_{13}=91, H_{14}=105$ implies $k=14$, so we can count on a profit of at most $100-(14+1)=85$ forints. A possible measurement sequence is:

$$
a_{1}=14, \quad a_{2}=13, \ldots, a_{10}=5, \quad a_{11}=3, \quad a_{12}=0, \quad a_{13}=0, \quad a_{14}=2
$$

Remarks. 1. After some calculations, it turns out that for $n$ balls, the achievable profit is

$$
\left[\frac{2 n-1-\sqrt{8 n-7}}{2}\right] \text { forints. }
$$

2. In the solution, we sought the profit that we can achieve even in the "worst" case. We could also examine what the maximum expected profit is. This is not an easy question; here we only illustrate what it means with an example.

The measurement is performed by dividing the balls into piles of sizes $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{k}$, and then sending the piles of sizes $a_{1}, a_{2}$, etc., for measurement (except the last one). If the radioactive ball is in the $i$-th pile - the probability of which is $a_{i} / n$, our loss is $a_{i}+i$. Thus, the expected value of the loss is

$$
\frac{a_{1}}{n}\left(1+a_{1}\right)+\frac{a_{2}}{n}\left(2+a_{2}\right)+\ldots+\frac{a_{k-1}}{n}\left(k-1+a_{k-1}\right)+\frac{a_{k}}{n}\left(k-1+a_{k}\right)
$$

For 100 balls with the grouping described in the solution, this value is

$$
\begin{gathered}
\frac{14}{100}(14+1)+\frac{13}{100}(13+2)+\ldots+\frac{5}{100}(5+10)+ \\
+\frac{3}{100}(3+11)+\frac{2}{100}(2+11)=14.93
\end{gathered}
$$

Thus, the expected value of the loss is slightly less than 15, which is natural, since in two percent of the cases, it is already clear after 11 measurements that the remaining balls include the radioactive one.

One of the optimal groupings is the following:

$$
\begin{gathered}
a_{1}=10, a_{2}=a_{3}=9, a_{4}=a_{5}=8, a_{6}=a_{7}=7, a_{8}=a_{9}=6, a_{10}=a_{11}=5 \\
a_{12}=a_{13}=4, a_{14}=a_{15}=3, a_{16}=a_{17}=a_{18}=2
\end{gathered}
$$

In this case, it is possible that our loss exceeds 15 forints, but the probability of this is small. If, however, the radioactive ball is found in one of the first 7 measurements, the loss is only 13 or 14 forints, so it is worth taking the risk. The expected value in this case is 13.84 forints, which means that on average, we can win about 1 forint more than before.

question: Let $ f(t)$ be a continuous function on the interval $ 0 \leq t \leq 1$, and define the two sets of points \[ A_t\equal{}\{(t,0): t\in[0,1]\} , B_t\equal{}\{(f(t),1): t\in [0,1]\}.\] Show that the union of all segments $ \overline{A_tB_t}$ is Lebesgue-measurable, and find the minimum of its measure with respect to all functions $ f$. [A. Csaszar]

meta.gold_solution:
1. **Show that the set \( A = \bigcup_{0 \le t \le 1} \overline{A_tB_t} \) is closed:**

   - Let \( P_n \) be a convergent sequence of points in \( A \), such that \( P_n \to P_0 \).
   - By the definition of \( A \), for every \( n \), there exists a \( t_n \) such that \( P_n \in \overline{A_{t_n}B_{t_n}} \).
   - According to the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem, the sequence \( t_n \) contains a convergent subsequence: \( t_{n_k} \to t_0 \).
   - The distance from the point \( P_{n_k} \) to the segment \( \overline{A_{t_0}B_{t_0}} \) is not greater than \( \max \{|f(t_{n_k}) - f(t_0)|, |t_{n_k} - t_0|\} \), which tends to \( 0 \) by the continuity of \( f(t) \).
   - Since \( A \) contains the limit point of any convergent sequence of its points, \( A \) is closed.

2. **Show that the set \( A \) is Lebesgue-measurable:**

   - Since \( A \) is closed, it is also Lebesgue-measurable.

3. **Determine the minimum measure of \( A \):**

   - Consider the point on the segment \( \overline{A_tB_t} \) that lies on the straight line \( y = c \). The abscissa of this point is \( (1 - c)t + cf(t) \), which is a continuous function of \( t \) due to the continuity of \( f(t) \).
   - Consequently, if two points of the set \( A \) lie on the line \( y = c \), then \( A \) contains the segment that joins these points.

4. **Calculate the measure of \( A \) for different functions \( f(t) \):**

   - If \( f(t) \) is constant, then \( A \) is a triangle of unit base and unit altitude, so it has measure \( \frac{1}{2} \).
   - If the segments \( \overline{A_0B_0} \) and \( \overline{A_1B_1} \) do not intersect, then the trapezoid with vertices \( A_0 \), \( B_0 \), \( A_1 \), and \( B_1 \) is a subset of \( A \), so the measure of \( A \) is not less than \( \frac{1}{2} \).
   - If the segments \( \overline{A_0B_0} \) and \( \overline{A_1B_1} \) intersect at some point \( C \), then the triangles \( A_0CA_1 \) and \( B_0CB_1 \) are subsets of \( A \), so the measure of \( A \) is not smaller than:
     \[
     t(d) = \frac{1}{2}\left( \frac{1}{1 + d} + \frac{d}{1 + d}d \right) = \frac{1}{2}\frac{1 + d^2}{1 + d},
     \]
     where \( d \) denotes the distance from \( B_0 \) to \( B_1 \).

5. **Find the minimum of \( t(d) \):**

   - By a simple calculation, we obtain that the minimum of \( t(d) \) on the positive half-axis is \( \sqrt{2} - 1 \).
   - Thus, the measure of \( A \) cannot be less than \( \sqrt{2} - 1 \).
   - On the other hand, for \( f(t) = (\sqrt{2} - 1)(1 - t) \), the measure of \( A \) is exactly \( \sqrt{2} - 1 \).

\(\blacksquare\)

The final answer is \( \boxed{ \sqrt{2} - 1 } \).

At the beginning of the school year, Heinz bought two different types of notebooks, one costing 8 Pf, the other 15 Pf per piece. He paid 1.31 MDN for 12 notebooks in total.

How many notebooks did he buy of each type?

meta.gold_solution:
Let $a$ be the number of notebooks costing 8 Pf and $b$ the number of notebooks costing 15 Pf. Then we have

$$
a \cdot 8 + b \cdot 15 = 131 \quad ; \quad a + b = 12 \quad \text{or} \quad a = 12 - b
$$

Substituting the second equation into the first, we get $8 \cdot (12 - b) + 15b = 131$. From this, we find $b = 5$ and further $a = 7$.

Heinz buys 7 notebooks costing 8 Pf and 5 notebooks costing 15 Pf.

Let $n \geqslant 2$ be an integer, and let $A_{n}$ be the set  
$$ A_{n}=\left\{2^{n}-2^{k} \mid k \in \mathbb{Z}, 0 \leqslant k<n\right\} . $$  
Determine the largest positive integer that cannot be written as the sum of one or more (not necessarily distinct) elements of $A_{n}$. (Serbia)

For $n=2$, the set $A_{n}$ consists of the two elements 2 and 3. Every positive integer $m$ except for 1 can be represented as the sum of elements of $A_{n}$ in this case: as $m=2+2+\cdots+2$ if $m$ is even, and as $m=3+2+2+\cdots+2$ if $m$ is odd. Now consider some $n>2$, and take an integer $m>(n-2) 2^{n}+1$. If $m$ is even, then consider 
$$ \frac{m}{2} \geqslant \frac{(n-2) 2^{n}+2}{2}=(n-2) 2^{n-1}+1>(n-3) 2^{n-1}+1 $$
By the induction hypothesis, there is a representation of the form 
$$ \frac{m}{2}=\left(2^{n-1}-2^{k_{1}}\right)+\left(2^{n-1}-2^{k_{2}}\right)+\cdots+\left(2^{n-1}-2^{k_{r}}\right) $$
for some $k_{i}$ with $0 \leqslant k_{i}<n-1$. It follows that 
$$ m=\left(2^{n}-2^{k_{1}+1}\right)+\left(2^{n}-2^{k_{2}+1}\right)+\cdots+\left(2^{n}-2^{k_{r}+1}\right) $$
giving us the desired representation of $m$. If $m$ is odd, then consider

question: Let $a$ and $b$ be positive integers. When $a^{2}+b^{2}$ is divided by $a+b,$ the quotient is $q$ and the remainder is $r.$ Find all pairs $(a,b)$ such that $q^{2}+r=1977$.

meta.gold_solution:
1. Given that \(a\) and \(b\) are positive integers, and when \(a^2 + b^2\) is divided by \(a + b\), the quotient is \(q\) and the remainder is \(r\). This can be expressed as:
   \[
   a^2 + b^2 = q(a + b) + r
   \]
   where \(0 \leq r < a + b\).

2. We are given that \(q^2 + r = 1977\). We need to find pairs \((a, b)\) such that this condition holds.

3. From the inequality \(0 \leq r < a + b\), we can infer that:
   \[
   q^2 < 1977 \implies q < \sqrt{1977} \approx 44.45
   \]
   Since \(q\) is an integer, \(q \leq 44\).

4. If \(q = 44\), then:
   \[
   r = 1977 - q^2 = 1977 - 44^2 = 1977 - 1936 = 41
   \]
   Therefore, we have \(q = 44\) and \(r = 41\).

5. Substituting \(q = 44\) and \(r = 41\) into the equation \(a^2 + b^2 = q(a + b) + r\), we get:
   \[
   a^2 + b^2 = 44(a + b) + 41
   \]
   Rearranging this, we have:
   \[
   a^2 + b^2 - 44(a + b) = 41
   \]
   Completing the square, we get:
   \[
   (a - 22)^2 + (b - 22)^2 = 1009
   \]
   Here, \(1009\) is a prime number, and it can be expressed as the sum of two squares in only one way:
   \[
   1009 = 28^2 + 15^2
   \]

6. Therefore, the pairs \((a - 22, b - 22)\) can be \((28, 15)\) or \((15, 28)\). This gives us the pairs:
   \[
   (a, b) = (50, 37) \quad \text{or} \quad (a, b) = (37, 50)
   \]

The final answer is \( \boxed{ (a, b) = (50, 37) } \) or \((a, b) = (37, 50)\).

Find all functions $f : \mathbb{N} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that for all triples $a,b,c$ of positive integers the following holds :

$$f(ac)+f(bc)-f(c)f(ab) \ge 1$$

Proposed by [i]Mojtaba Zare[/i]

meta.gold_solution:
1. Let \( P(a, b, c) \) be the inequality:
   \[
   f(ac) + f(bc) - f(c)f(ab) \geq 1 \quad \forall \, a, b, c \in \mathbb{N}.
   \]

2. Consider \( P(1, 1, 1) \):
   \[
   f(1 \cdot 1) + f(1 \cdot 1) - f(1)f(1 \cdot 1) \geq 1 \implies 2f(1) - f(1)^2 \geq 1.
   \]
   Solving the quadratic inequality:
   \[
   f(1)^2 - 2f(1) + 1 \leq 0 \implies (f(1) - 1)^2 \leq 0 \implies f(1) = 1.
   \]

3. Consider \( P(a, b, 1) \):
   \[
   f(a \cdot 1) + f(b \cdot 1) - f(1)f(ab) \geq 1 \implies f(a) + f(b) - f(ab) \geq 1 \quad \forall \, a, b \in \mathbb{N}.
   \]

4. Consider \( P(a, 1, b) \):
   \[
   f(ab) + f(b) - f(b)f(a) \geq 1 \quad \forall \, a, b \in \mathbb{N}.
   \]

5. Adding the two inequalities from steps 3 and 4:
   \[
   f(a) + f(b) - f(ab) + f(ab) + f(b) - f(b)f(a) \geq 2 \implies f(a) + 2f(b) - f(a)f(b) \geq 2.
   \]
   Rearranging:
   \[
   (f(a) - 2)(f(b) - 1) \leq 0 \quad \forall \, a, b \in \mathbb{N}.
   \]
   This implies:
   \[
   1 \leq f(x) \leq 2 \quad \forall \, x \in \mathbb{N}.
   \]

6. Now, we will prove \( f \equiv 1 \). Let \( k \leq 2 \) be an upper bound of \( f \).

7. Setting \( f(c) = f(ab) = k \) in the original equation:
   \[
   f(ac) + f(bc) \geq k^2 + 1.
   \]
   Since \( 1 \leq f(x) \leq 2 \), we have:
   \[
   k^2 + 1 \leq 4 \implies k \leq \sqrt{3} \implies 1 \leq f(x) \leq \sqrt{3}.
   \]

8. Similarly, setting \( f(c) = f(ab) = k \) in the original equation:
   \[
   f(ac) + f(bc) \geq k^2 + 1 \implies k^2 + 1 \leq 2\sqrt{3} \implies k \leq \sqrt{2\sqrt{3} - 1}.
   \]
   Hence:
   \[
   1 \leq f(x) \leq \sqrt{2\sqrt{3} - 1}.
   \]

9. Let \( g(x) = \sqrt{2x - 1} \). Then, by induction, it holds:
   \[
   k \leq \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} g^n(2).
   \]
   In fact, the value of such limit is \( 1 \).

   Proof: Let \( h(n) = g^{(n)}(2) \). Clearly, \( h \) is decreasing and lowerly bounded \((g \geq 0 \implies h \geq 0)\). Hence, \( h \) converges in \( \mathbb{R} \). Let \( r \) be the value to which it converges. Then:
   \[
   r = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} h(n) = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} g^{(n)}(2) = \lim_{(n-1) \rightarrow \infty} g(g^{(n-1)}(2)) = g(\lim_{(n-1) \rightarrow \infty} g^{(n-1)}(2)) = g(r).
   \]
   Thus:
   \[
   r = g(r) \implies r = \sqrt{2r - 1} \implies r = 1.
   \]

10. Now, we know:
    \[
    \max f = k \leq 1.
    \]
    But indeed:
    \[
    1 \leq f(x) \leq 2.
    \]

Therefore, \( \boxed{f \equiv 1} \), which indeed fits.

Therefore, the sequence $\left\{a_{n}\right\}$, if it exists, is unique.
Every natural number $n$ can be represented in binary as
$$
n=d_{k} \cdot 2^{k}+d_{k-1} \cdot 2^{k-1}+\cdots+d_{1} \cdot 2+d_{0},
$$

Consider the sequence
$$
a_{n}=d_{k} \cdot 8^{k}+d_{k-1} \cdot 8^{k-1}+\cdots+d_{1} \cdot 8+d_{0}.
$$

where $d_{i}(i=0,1, \cdots, k) \in\{0,1\}, k \in N \cup\{0\}$.

$$
m=c_{s} \cdot 8^{s}+c_{s-1} \cdot 8^{s-1}+\cdots+c_{1} \cdot 8+c_{0},
$$

where $c_{i} \in\{0,1, \cdots, 7\}, 0 \leqslant i \leqslant s, s \in N \cup\{0\}$.
Each $c_{i} \in\{0,1, \cdots, 7\}$ can be uniquely expressed as
$$
c_{i}=d_{i}+2 d_{j}+4 d_{k}, d_{i}, d_{j}, d_{k} \in\{0,1\}
$$

Therefore, $m$ can be expressed as
$$
m=a_{i}+2 a_{j}+4 a_{k}

where $a_{i}, a_{j}, a_{k}$ have the form (1), and $a_{i}, a_{j}, a_{k}$ are uniquely determined by (2).
On the other hand, if there is (3), where $a_{i}, a_{j}, a_{k}$ have the form (1), then by the uniqueness of octal representation, their coefficients are uniquely determined by (2), and thus the representation of $m$ is unique.

question:
Determine all pairs $(a, b)$ of positive integers for which

$$
a^{2}+b \mid a^{2} b+a \quad \text { and } \quad b^{2}-a \mid a b^{2}+b .
$$

meta.gold_solution:
From $a^{2}+b \mid a^{2} b+a$ it follows

$$
a^{2}+b \mid\left(a^{2} b+a\right)-b\left(a^{2}+b\right)=a-b^{2}
$$

From $b^{2}-a \mid a b^{2}+b$ it follows

$$
b^{2}-a \mid\left(a b^{2}+b\right)-a\left(b^{2}-a\right)=b+a^{2} .
$$

We see that $a^{2}+b\left|a-b^{2}\right| a^{2}+b$. This means that $a^{2}+b$ is equal to $a-b^{2}$ up to a sign. Therefore, we have two cases: $a^{2}+b=b^{2}-a$ and $a^{2}+b=a-b^{2}$. In the second case, $a^{2}+b^{2}=a-b$. But $a^{2} \geq a$ and $b^{2} \geq b>-b$, so this is impossible. Therefore, we must have the first case: $a^{2}+b=b^{2}-a$. This gives $a^{2}-b^{2}=-a-b$, so $(a+b)(a-b)=-(a+b)$. Since $a+b$ is positive, we can divide by it and get $a-b=-1$, so $b=a+1$. All pairs that can satisfy the conditions are thus of the form $(a, a+1)$ for a positive integer $a$.
We check these pairs. We have $a^{2}+b=a^{2}+a+1$ and $a^{2} b+a=a^{2}(a+1)+a=$ $a^{3}+a^{2}+a=a\left(a^{2}+a+1\right)$, so the first divisibility relation is satisfied. Furthermore, $b^{2}-a=(a+1)^{2}-a=a^{2}+a+1$ and $a b^{2}+b=a(a+1)^{2}+(a+1)=a^{3}+2 a^{2}+2 a+1=$ $a\left(a^{2}+a+1\right)+a^{2}+a+1=(a+1)\left(a^{2}+a+1\right)$, so the second divisibility relation is also satisfied. The pairs $(a, a+1)$ thus satisfy the conditions and are therefore the exact solutions.

For every integer $n \ge 1$, the function $f_n : \left\{ 0, 1, \cdots, n \right\} \to \mathbb R$ is defined recursively by $f_n(0) = 0$, $f_n(1) = 1$ and \[ (n-k) f_n(k-1) + kf_n(k+1) = nf_n(k) \] for each $1 \le k < n$.  Let $S_N = f_{N+1}(1) + f_{N+2}(2) + \cdots + f_{2N} (N)$. Find the remainder when $\left\lfloor S_{2013} \right\rfloor$ is divided by $2011$.  (Here $\left\lfloor x \right\rfloor$ is the greatest integer not exceeding $x$.)

[i]Proposed by Lewis Chen[/i]

meta.gold_solution:
1. **Define the function \( f_n(k) \) recursively:**
   Given the recursive definition:
   \[
   f_n(0) = 0, \quad f_n(1) = 1, \quad \text{and} \quad (n-k) f_n(k-1) + k f_n(k+1) = n f_n(k) \quad \text{for} \quad 1 \le k < n
   \]
   We need to find a general form for \( f_n(k) \).

2. **Identify a pattern:**
   By examining the given recursive relation, we hypothesize that:
   \[
   f_n(k) = \sum_{i=1}^k \binom{n}{i-1}
   \]
   This hypothesis can be verified by induction, but for now, we will use it to proceed with the problem.

3. **Express \( S_N \) in terms of binomial coefficients:**
   \[
   S_N = f_{N+1}(1) + f_{N+2}(2) + \cdots + f_{2N}(N)
   \]
   Using the hypothesized form of \( f_n(k) \):
   \[
   S_N = \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{j=1}^i \binom{N+i}{j-1}
   \]

4. **Simplify the double sum:**
   Rewriting the double sum:
   \[
   S_N = \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{j=0}^{i-1} \binom{N+i}{j}
   \]
   Using the Hockey Stick Identity:
   \[
   \sum_{j=0}^{i-1} \binom{N+i}{j} = \binom{N+i+1}{i}
   \]
   Therefore:
   \[
   S_N = \sum_{i=1}^N \binom{N+i+1}{i}
   \]

5. **Further simplification using binomial identities:**
   Recognize that:
   \[
   \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} \binom{2N}{i} = 2^{2N-1} - \binom{2N-1}{N-1}
   \]
   Thus:
   \[
   2S_N + \binom{2N}{N} = 2^{2N}
   \]

6. **Solve for \( S_N \):**
   \[
   2S_N = 2^{2N} - \binom{2N}{N}
   \]
   \[
   S_N = \frac{2^{2N} - \binom{2N}{N}}{2}
   \]

7. **Calculate \( S_{2013} \) modulo 2011:**
   \[
   2^{2 \cdot 2013} \equiv 64 \pmod{2011}
   \]
   \[
   \binom{2 \cdot 2013}{2013} \equiv 12 \pmod{2011}
   \]
   Therefore:
   \[
   S_{2013} = \frac{64 - 12}{2} = 26 \pmod{2011}
   \]

The final answer is \( \boxed{26} \).

Example 1, find the tangent line equation at a point $\left(x_{0}, y_{0}\right)$ on a general quadratic curve (non-degenerate case);
$$
\mathrm{Ax}^{2}+\mathrm{Bxy}+\mathrm{Cy}^{2}+\mathrm{Dx}+\mathrm{Ey}+\mathrm{F}=0
$$

meta.gold_solution:
Solve: Express $y$ as an implicit function of $x$, differentiate both sides of equation (5) with respect to $x$, we get
$$
\begin{array}{l}
2 A x + B y + B x y' + 2 C y y' + D + E y' = 0, \\
\text { i.e., } y' = \frac{-(2 A x + B y + D)}{2 C y + B x + E}, \\
\left.\therefore \quad y'\right|_{(x_0, y_0)} = -\frac{2 A x_0 + B y_0 + D}{2 C y_0 + B x_0 + E} \\
\end{array}
$$

Thus, by equation (2), the equation of the tangent line is:
$$
y - y_0 = -\frac{2 A x_0 + B y_0 + D}{2 C y_0 + B x_0 + E}(x - x_0),
$$

Simplifying, we get
$$
\begin{array}{l}
2 A x_0 x + B x_0 y + B y_0 x + 2 C y_0 y + D x + E y \\
- (2 A x_0^2 + 2 B x_0 y_0 + 2 C y_0^2 + D x_0 + E y_0) \\
= 0,
\end{array}
$$

But the point $(x_0, y_0)$ lies on the curve (5), so it must satisfy this equation, i.e.,
$$
\begin{aligned}
& A x_0^2 + B x_0 y_0 + C y_0^2 + D x_0 + E y_0 + F = 0, \\
\therefore \quad & 2 A x_0^2 + 2 B x_0 y_0 + 2 C y_0^2 \\
& = -2 D x_0 - 2 E y_0 - 2 F.
\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above equation into (6), we get
$$
\begin{array}{l}
2 A x_0 x + B x_0 y + B y_0 x + 2 C y_0 y + D (x + x_0) \\
+ E (y + y_0) + 2 F = 0,
\end{array}
$$

i.e.,
$$
A x_0 x + \frac{B}{2} (x_0 y + y_0 x) + C y_0 y + \frac{D}{2} (x + x_0) + \frac{E}{2} (y + y_0) + F = 0
$$

is the required tangent line equation.
In the above example, comparing equations (5) and (7), we can see: to find the tangent line equation of a quadratic curve (5) at a point $(x_0, y_0)$ on the curve, we only need to replace $x^2, xy, y^2, x, y$ in equation (5) with $x_0 x, \frac{x_0 y + y_0 x}{2}, y_0 y, \frac{x_0 + x}{2}, \frac{y_0 + y}{2}$, respectively, and we can directly obtain the tangent line equation (7). From this, we can easily derive the tangent line equations for standard forms of ellipses, hyperbolas, and parabolas:
Ellipse $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$, tangent line $\frac{x_0 x}{a^2} + \frac{y_0 y}{b^2} = 1$;
Hyperbola $\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$, tangent line $\frac{x_0 x}{a^2} - \frac{y_0 y}{b^2} = 1$;
Parabola $y^2 = 2 p x$, tangent line $y_0 y = p (x_0 + x)$.

question: Determine all real numbers $x, y, z$ satisfying the following system of equations: $x=\sqrt{2 y+3}, y=\sqrt{2 z+3}, z=\sqrt{2 x+3}$.

It is clear that the numbers $x, y, z$ must be strictly positive. The first two equations give $x^{2}=2 y+3$ and $y^{2}=2 z+3$. By subtracting them, we obtain $x^{2}-y^{2}=2(y-z)$. From this, we deduce that if $x \leqslant y$ then $y \leqslant z$, and similarly if $y \leqslant z$ then $z \leqslant x$. Therefore, if $x \leqslant y$, we have $x \leqslant y \leqslant z \leqslant x$, which implies that $x=y=z$.

We can similarly show that if $x \geqslant y$ then $x=y=z$. Therefore, in all cases, $x, y, z$ are equal, and their common value satisfies the equation $x^{2}=2 x+3$, which can also be written as $(x-3)(x+1)=0$. Since $x$ is strictly positive, it must be that $x=y=z=3$. Conversely, it is immediately verified that $x=y=z=3$ is indeed a solution to the system.

9.4. In the company, some pairs of people are friends (if $A$ is friends with $B$, then $B$ is also friends with $A$). It turned out that among any 100 people in the company, the number of pairs of friends is odd. Find the largest possible number of people in such a company.

(E. Bakayev)

meta.gold_solution:
Answer: 101.

Solution: In all solutions below, we consider the friendship graph, where vertices are people in the company, and two people are connected by an edge if they are friends.

If the graph is a cycle containing 101 vertices, then any 100 vertices will have exactly 99 edges, so such a company satisfies the conditions of the problem. It remains to show that there cannot be a company of 102 people (then a company of more than 102 people cannot exist either). Below we provide several different ways to do this; in each way, we assume, for the sake of contradiction, that such a company has been found.

First solution. Consider an arbitrary set of 101 vertices and the induced subgraph on these vertices, let it have $k$ edges. By removing an arbitrary vertex from this subgraph (say, of degree $d$), we get 100 vertices with an odd number of edges $k-d$. Thus, the degree of any vertex in our subgraph has a parity different from the parity of $k$, meaning that the degrees of all vertices in the subgraph have the same parity. However, as is well known, in a graph with an odd number of vertices, all vertices cannot have an odd degree. Therefore, all these degrees are even, and the number of edges $k$ is odd.

Now let the entire graph with 102 vertices have $\ell$ edges. When any vertex (say, of degree $d$) is removed, we get a subgraph with an odd number of edges $\ell-d$; similarly to the above reasoning, we get that in the entire graph, all vertices have the same parity of degrees. Note that our graph cannot be empty (i.e., have no edges) or complete (i.e., have all $C_{102}^{2}$ edges), otherwise, on any 100 vertices, there will be either 0 or $C_{100}^{2}=99 \cdot 50$ edges, which is an even number. Therefore, there is a vertex connected to at least one other vertex but not to all. In other words, there are vertices $u, v_{1}$, and $v_{2}$ such that $u$ is connected to $v_{1}$ but not to $v_{2}$. The degrees of vertices $v_{1}$ and $v_{2}$ in the original graph have the same parity, so after removing $u$, they will have different parities. This is impossible by the above proof.

Second solution. There are $n=C_{102}^{2}=51 \cdot 101$ ways to remove two vertices from 102, leaving 100. Number these ways from 1 to $n$. Let $a_{i}$ be the number of edges on the remaining 100 vertices in the $i$-th way; by assumption, all numbers $a_{i}$ are odd, and thus their sum $S$ is also odd (since the number $n$ is odd).

On the other hand, consider any edge $uv$. This edge is counted in the number $a_{i}$ exactly when vertices $u$ and $v$ are not removed in the $i$-th way, i.e., when some pair of the remaining 100 vertices is removed. This happens in $k=C_{100}^{2}=50 \cdot 99$ ways. Thus, each edge is counted in $S$ an even number of times $k$, so $S$ must be even. Contradiction.

Third solution. Call a vertex even if its degree is even, and odd otherwise. Consider two cases.

Case 1. Suppose the total number of edges in the graph is odd. Then, by removing any pair of vertices, we must remove an even number of edges (to leave an odd number). On the other hand, if we remove vertices with degrees $d_{1}$ and $d_{2}$, the number of removed edges is $d_{1}+d_{2}$ if these vertices are not connected by an edge, and $d_{1}+d_{2}-1$ if they are connected. Therefore, vertices of the same parity are never connected by an edge, and vertices of different parities are always connected.

Thus, if the graph has $k$ even vertices and $\ell$ odd vertices, even vertices have (even) degree $\ell$, and odd vertices have (odd) degree $k$. This is impossible, since $k+\ell=102$.

Case 2. Suppose the total number of edges in the graph is even. Similarly, we get that vertices of the same parity are always connected by an edge, and vertices of different parities are never connected. Therefore, if the graph has $k$ even vertices and $\ell$ odd vertices, even vertices have (even) degree $k-1$, and odd vertices have (odd) degree $\ell-1$. This again contradicts the equality $k+\ell=102$.

$$

$$

$$

$$

## Definition 3.3.1.

Let $G$ be a non-empty set with a binary operation: for every pair $a, b \in G$, there is an element $a b \in G$. Then we say that $G$ is a group if the following axioms are satisfied.

1. (Associativity) For all $a, b, c \in G(a b) c=a(b c)$.
2. (Identity element) There exists $e \in G$ such that for all $a \in G e a=a$ and $a e=a$.
3. (Invertibility) For all $a \in G$, there exists a (unique) $a^{-1} \in G$ such that $a a^{-1}=e$ and $a^{-1} a=e$.

## Definition 3.3.2.

We say that $G$ is an abelian (or commutative) group if it also satisfies the following property

1. For all $a, b \in G, a b=b a$.

## Notation.

In the case of abelian groups, we often use the sign + for the binary operation, writing $a+b$ instead of $a b$. In this case, we also denote 0 as the identity element and $-a$ as the inverse of $a$.

## Example 3.3.3.

All the following examples are groups:

1. The set of integers with addition (abelian).
2. The set of non-zero real numbers with multiplication (abelian).
3. The set of translations in the plane forms a group (is it abelian?).

If $A$ and $B$ are two subsets of $G$, we denote

We say that a subset $H$ of $G$ is a subgroup of $G$ if it is a group with the binary operation of $G$.

## Definition 3.3.5.

If $H$ is a subgroup of $G$ and $a \in G$, $a H$ (resp. $Ha$) is called the left (resp. right) coset generated by $H$.

## Definition 3.3.6.

A subgroup $H$ of $G$ is said to be normal if for all $a \in G$ we have $a H=H a$.

## Remark 3.3.7.

If $G$ is abelian, all subgroups are normal.

## Theorem 3.3.8.

If $H$ is a normal subgroup of $G$, then the cosets generated by $H$ form a group with the binary operation

$$
(a H)(b H)=(a b H)
$$

We call this group the quotient group and denote it by $G / H$.

Let $n$ be a natural number, the groups $H=n \mathbb{Z}$ are normal subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}$. The quotient group $\mathbb{Z} / n \mathbb{Z}$ are the integers modulo $n$.

Theorem 3.3.11 (Lagrange's Theorem).

If $H$ is a subgroup of a finite group $G$, then $|H|$ divides $|G|$.

question: There is a very popular race course where runners frequently go for a daily run. Assume that all runners randomly select a start time, a starting position on the course, and a direction to run. Also assume that all runners make exactly one complete circuit of the race course, all runners run at the same speed, and all runners complete the circuit in one hour. Suppose that one afternoon you go for a run on this race course, and you count $300$ runners which you pass going in the opposite direction, although some of those runners you count twice since you pass them twice. What is the expected value of the number of different runners that you pass not counting duplicates?

   - You are running on a race course for 1 hour.
   - You pass 300 runners going in the opposite direction.
   - Some of these runners are counted twice because you pass them twice.
   - We need to find the expected number of different runners you pass, not counting duplicates.

2. **Splitting the Problem into Two Cases:**
   - Since each lap takes 1 hour and you are on the course for exactly 1 hour, we can split the problem into two 30-minute intervals.
   - In the first 30 minutes, if you see a runner, there is a $\frac{1}{2}$ chance that you will see them again in the next 30 minutes.

3. **Calculating the Expected Number of Runners in the First 30 Minutes:**
   - You pass 300 runners in total.
   - Since the runners are uniformly distributed, you would expect to pass half of them in the first 30 minutes.
   - Therefore, the expected number of runners you pass in the first 30 minutes is $\frac{300}{2} = 150$.

4. **Calculating the Expected Number of Runners Seen Again:**
   - Out of these 150 runners, there is a $\frac{1}{2}$ chance of seeing each one again in the next 30 minutes.
   - Therefore, the expected number of runners you see again is $\frac{150}{2} = 75$.

5. **Calculating the Expected Number of New Runners in the Second 30 Minutes:**
   - In the second 30 minutes, you again pass 150 runners.
   - Out of these 150 runners, 75 are those you saw in the first 30 minutes.
   - Therefore, the expected number of new runners you see in the second 30 minutes is $150 - 75 = 75$.

6. **Summing Up the Expected Number of Different Runners:**
   - The total expected number of different runners you pass is the sum of the runners you see in the first 30 minutes and the new runners you see in the second 30 minutes.
   - Therefore, the expected number of different runners is $150 + 75 = 225$.

\[

9. (40 points) Among nine visually identical gold coins, one weighs $a$, seven weigh $b$, and the last one weighs $c$, and $a < b < c$. Using a balance scale, find the minimum number of weighings required to identify the coin weighing $a$ and the coin weighing $c$.

To solve this problem, we need to devise a strategy to identify the coins with weights $a$ and $c$ using the fewest number of weighings. Here is a step-by-step approach:

1. **First Weighing:**
   - Divide the nine coins into three groups of three coins each: Group 1, Group 2, and Group 3.
   - Weigh Group 1 against Group 2.

   **Case 1:** If Group 1 and Group 2 balance, then the coin weighing $a$ and the coin weighing $c$ must be in Group 3.
   - Weigh two coins from Group 3 against each other.
     - If they balance, the remaining coin in Group 3 is the one weighing $c$.
     - If they do not balance, the lighter coin is the one weighing $a$ and the heavier coin is the one weighing $c$.

   **Case 2:** If Group 1 and Group 2 do not balance, then the coin weighing $a$ and the coin weighing $c$ are in the lighter and heavier groups, respectively.
   - Identify the lighter group (Group 1 or Group 2) and the heavier group (Group 1 or Group 2).
   - Weigh two coins from the lighter group against each other.
     - If they balance, the remaining coin in the lighter group is the one weighing $a$.
     - If they do not balance, the lighter coin is the one weighing $a$.
   - Weigh two coins from the heavier group against each other.
     - If they balance, the remaining coin in the heavier group is the one weighing $c$.
     - If they do not balance, the heavier coin is the one weighing $c$.

In both cases, we can identify the coins weighing $a$ and $c$ in a minimum of 2 weighings.

Thus, the minimum number of weighings required is \(\boxed{2}\).

$A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I$.
Weigh $(A, B, C, D)$ against $(E, F, G, H)$. If they balance, then $a+c=2b$. If they do not balance, assume without loss of generality that $(A, B, C, D) > (E, F, G, H)$.

For the second weighing, weigh $(A, B)$ against $(C, D)$ and $(E, F)$ against $(G, H)$. At this point, there are four possible scenarios:
(1) $(A, B) > (C, D)$ and $(E, F) > (G, H)$. Then the heavy coin is in $(A, B)$, and the light coin can only be in $(G, H)$. For the fourth weighing, place $(A, B, G, H)$ on one side and $(C, D, E, F)$ on the other side. The lightness or heaviness or balance of $(A, B, G, H)$ side indicates whether $a+c$ is lighter, heavier, or equal to $2b$.
(2) $(A, B) > (C, D)$ and $(E, F) = (G, H)$. Then the heavy coin is in $(A, B)$, and the light coin can only be in $(C, D, I)$.

If the light coin is in $(C, D)$, then it is already known that $a+c > 2b$. For the fourth weighing, place $(A, B, I)$ on one side and $(E, F, G)$ on the other side. The lightness or heaviness of the $(A, B, I)$ side indicates whether $a+c$ is lighter or heavier than $2b$.
(3) $(A, B) = (C, D)$ and $(E, F) > (G, H)$. Then the light coin is in $(G, H)$, and the heavy coin can only be in $(E, F, I)$. If the heavy coin is in $(E, F)$, then it is already known that $a+c < 2b$. For the fourth weighing, place $(A, B, C)$ on one side and $(G, H, I)$ on the other side. The lightness or heaviness or balance of the $(G, H, I)$ side indicates whether $a+c$ is lighter, heavier, or equal to $2b$.
(4) If both weighings are unbalanced, assume $(A, B) > (C, D)$ and $(E, F) > (G, H)$. For the third weighing, compare $(A, B)$ with $(G, H)$. If they balance, then the fake coins are in $(C, D, E, F)$. For the fourth weighing, compare $(A, B, G, H)$ with $(C, D, E, F)$. The lightness or heaviness or balance of the $(C, D, E, F)$ side indicates whether $a+c$ is lighter, heavier, or equal to $2b$; if they do not balance, then the fake coins are in $(A, B, G, H)$. For the fourth weighing, compare $(A, B, G, H)$ with $(C, D, E, F)$. The lightness or heaviness or balance of the $(A, B, G, H)$ side indicates whether $a+c$ is lighter, heavier, or equal to $2b$. In summary, four weighings are sufficient to determine the result.

question: Let's inscribe a rectangle with the largest area in the ellipse $b^{2} x^{2}+a^{2} y^{2}=a^{2} b^{2}(a>b)$ (the sides of the rectangle are parallel to the major axes of the ellipse). In this rectangle, inscribe an ellipse whose major axes are equal to the sides of the rectangle. In the thus obtained ellipse, inscribe a rectangle with the largest area, and so on. What is the sum of the areas of the infinitely many rectangles and ellipses thus obtained?

meta.gold_solution:
The ellipse is formed from the principal circle by an orthogonal affine transformation; the characteristic of the transformation is: $\frac{b_{⿹ 勹}}{a}$. The area of the principal circle: $a^{2} \pi$, the area of the ellipse: $a^{2} \pi \cdot \frac{b}{a}=a b \pi$.

Inscribe a square in the principal circle, whose sides are parallel to the major axes of the ellipse. The area of the square: $2 a^{2}$. The affine transformation of this square is the largest area rectangle inscribed in the ellipse (whose sides are parallel to the major axes). In the affine transformation, the side of the square inscribed in the circle that is parallel to the $X$-axis remains the same: $a \sqrt{2}$; the other side, however, is $\frac{b}{a} \cdot a \sqrt{2}=b \sqrt{2}$. The area of the rectangle is $a \sqrt{2} \cdot b \sqrt{2}=2 a b\left(=2 a^{2} \cdot \frac{b}{a}\right)$.

The major axis of the ellipse inscribed in this rectangle is: $a \sqrt{2}$, the minor axis is $b \sqrt{2}$. The area of the ellipse: $\frac{1}{2} a \sqrt{2} \cdot \frac{1}{2} b \sqrt{2} \cdot \pi=\frac{2 a b}{4} \pi=\frac{a b}{2} \pi$. The largest area rectangle inscribed in this ellipse is: $2 \cdot \frac{a \sqrt{2}}{2} \cdot \frac{b \sqrt{2}}{2}=a b$.

From this, we can already see that the areas of the ellipses in question form an infinite geometric series whose first term is $a b \pi$, and whose common ratio is $\frac{1}{2}$. The sum of these is therefore $2 a b \pi$.

The largest area rectangles also form such a series; the first term of the series is: $2 a b$, the common ratio is $\frac{1}{2}$. The sum of these is $4 a b$.[^0]

Example 7 Select several colors from the given six different colors to color the six faces of a cube, with each face being colored with exactly one color, and any two faces sharing a common edge must be colored with different colors. How many different coloring schemes are there?

The remaining 4 colors are used to color the remaining four side faces (a circular permutation of 4 colors), which has \((4-1)!\) ways. Therefore, when all 6 colors are used, the number of coloring schemes is \( C_5^1 \cdot (4-1)! = 30 \).
(2) When exactly 5 colors are used. There are \( C_6^5 \) ways to choose 5 colors from 6 colors. At this point, there must be one pair of opposite faces with the same color. Choose 1 color from the 5 colors to color this pair of opposite faces, and place them facing up and down, which has \( C_5^1 \) ways. The remaining 4 colors are used to color the remaining four side faces (a necklace permutation of 4 different colored beads), which has \(\frac{(4-1)!}{2}\) ways. Therefore, when exactly 5 colors are used, the number of coloring schemes is
\[
C_6^5 \cdot C_5^1 \cdot \frac{1}{2}(4-1)! = 90 \text{ ways.}
\]
(3) When exactly 4 colors are used, there are \( C_6^4 \) ways to choose 4 colors from 6 colors. At this point, there must be 2 pairs of opposite faces with the same color, and one pair of opposite faces with different colors. Place the pair of opposite faces with different colors facing up and down, and choose 2 colors from the 4 colors to color the top and bottom faces (at this point, the top and bottom faces are indistinguishable), which has \( C_4^2 \) ways. The remaining 2 colors are used to color the remaining four side faces so that the 2 pairs of opposite faces have the same color (this can be seen as a necklace permutation of 2 colored beads, or a circular permutation), which has only 1 way. Therefore, when exactly 4 colors are used, the number of coloring schemes is \( C_6^4 \cdot C_4^2 \cdot 1 = 90 \) ways.
(4) When exactly 3 colors are used, there are \( C_6^3 \) ways to choose 3 colors from 6 colors. At this point, all 3 pairs of opposite faces have the same color, and using 3 colors to color them has only 1 way. Therefore, when exactly 3 colors are used, the number of coloring schemes is \( C_6^3 = 20 \) ways.
In summary, the total number of different coloring schemes is \( 30 + 90 + 90 + 20 = 230 \) ways.

& a+b_{1}=99 \ldots 9=10^{k}-1 \\

\end{aligned}
$$

\end{aligned}
